provenance.dataset: Petroleum spot prices (series RWTC and RBRTE)
provenance.cadence: Each business day, roughly a two business day publication lag.
provenance.reliability: Primary source. EIA is the originator; FRED merely republishes these same two series as DCOILWTICO and DCOILBRENTEU.
provenance.caveat: These are SPOT prices, not front-month futures. Spot and the futures screen you see on CNBC can differ by a dollar or more, and spot publishes with a lag while futures are live. Do not use this to time anything intraday.
provenance.lag_note: This source publishes about 6 days behind real time, so an observation that old is normal, not a broken feed. For same-session crude you would need a front-month futures feed, which is licensed.
provenance.quality_meaning: Fetched from the originating source. This is a real observation.

impact.meaning: This series cuts BOTH WAYS. A rise pushes mortgage rates UP through inflation expectations (path strength 33%) and DOWN through recession risk (path strength 16%). On current weights the inflation channel dominates, so the net effect of a rise is UP. The two can trade places depending on how far and how fast it moves: a modest rise is an inflation story, a violent one becomes a demand story.

chains.chain: Brent crude (global benchmark) → ↑ Inflation expectations → ↑ 10Y Treasury → ↑ MBS yield → ↑ 30Y mortgage rate
rationales: Brent prices roughly two thirds of the world’s traded crude, so it is the better read on GLOBAL inflation. Foreign inflation feeds foreign policy rates, which feeds the demand for US duration.
The 10Y is a real yield plus an inflation expectation. Expectations move the nominal.
MBS are priced off the Treasury curve. This is the main channel.
Lenders price off MBS execution, with a short lag for rate sheets.

chains.chain: Brent crude (global benchmark) → ↑ Recession risk → ↓ 10Y Treasury → ↓ MBS yield → ↓ 30Y mortgage rate
rationales: A sustained crude spike is a tax on the consumer. This is the offsetting channel: the same oil move that lifts inflation expectations also raises recession risk, and those two push mortgage rates in opposite directions.
Recession fear is the classic bid for duration. Yields fall.
MBS are priced off the Treasury curve. This is the main channel.
Lenders price off MBS execution, with a short lag for rate sheets.
